tools.name: workflows_get
tools.title: Get Workflow
tools.description: Get details for a saved workflow.

tools.name: workflows_create
tools.title: Create Workflow
tools.description:
Create and save a new Workflow in the workspace.

Validate the config before creating the workflow when
workflow_specs_validate is available. That validation tool requires a
Roboflow API key; OAuth users can use workflow_blocks_* tools for
schema inspection or agent_chat for guided workflow construction.

The config is the same JSON format used by the workflow specification
tools. Once saved, API-key sessions can execute the workflow by ID
with workflows_run.

Returns the created workflow including its document ID. Save
this ID — it is required for workflows_update.

business_context.description: Brief description of the business problem this workflow addresses, if the user has shared one.

tools.name: workflows_update
tools.title: Update Workflow
tools.description:
Update an existing saved Workflow's name and definition.

Validate the config before updating the workflow when
workflow_specs_validate is available. That validation tool requires a
Roboflow API key; OAuth users can use workflow_blocks_* tools for
schema inspection or agent_chat for guided workflow edits.

Use workflows_get to retrieve the current workflow first, then
modify the config as needed.

workflow_id.description: Workflow document ID — NOT the URL slug. Get it from workflows_list or workflows_create response.

tools.name: workflows_delete
tools.title: Delete Workflow
tools.description:
Delete a saved Workflow, moving it to the workspace Trash.

This is a soft delete: the workflow stays in the Trash for 30 days
and can be restored with ``trash_restore_workflow`` using the
workflow's document id from the delete response or ``trash_list``.
After 30 days it is permanently removed.

workflow_url.description: Workflow URL slug (the `url` field from workflows_list).

tools.name: workflow_blocks_list
tools.title: List Workflow Blocks
tools.description:
List all available Workflow blocks with a short summary of each.

Returns a list of blocks, each with manifest (schema key), name,
block_type, and short_description. Use ``workflow_blocks_get_schema``
to get the full schema of a specific block.

block_type.description: Filter by block category. If omitted, all blocks are returned.

tools.name: workflow_blocks_get_schema
tools.title: Get Workflow Block Schema
tools.description:
Get the full schema of a specific Workflow block.

Returns all properties, required fields, and descriptions for a
block identified by its manifest name (as returned by
``workflow_blocks_list``).

tools.name: workflow_specs_validate
tools.title: Validate Workflow Specification

specification.description: Full Workflow JSON definition with 'version', 'inputs', 'steps', and 'outputs'

tools.name: workflows_run
tools.title: Run Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a saved Workflow on one or more images.

Runs a previously created Workflow against the provided images on
the Roboflow serverless infrastructure. This always hits the
latest **published** version of the workflow.

IMPORTANT: Workflows created or edited via ``agent_chat`` are
saved as drafts, not published. If you want to run an agent's
latest changes, either call ``agent_workflow_publish`` first,
or pass the ``specification`` returned by ``agent_chat`` to
``workflow_specs_run`` to execute the draft directly.

Images are processed synchronously; calls with many images take
proportionally longer.

Returns workflow outputs as defined by the workflow's output blocks.

images.description: Map of input names to image values (HTTPS URLs or base64). Example: {'image': 'https://...'}

parameters.description: Optional runtime parameters (e.g. confidence thresholds, class filters)

tools.name: workflow_specs_run
tools.title: Run Workflow Specification
tools.description:
Execute a Workflow from an inline JSON definition.

Unlike ``workflows_run`` which runs a saved workflow by ID,
this tool accepts a full workflow JSON spec and executes it
directly. Useful for testing workflows before saving them, or
for running an agent-built draft without publishing — pass
the ``specification`` returned by ``agent_chat``.

Validate the definition with ``workflow_specs_validate`` before
running it; invalid specifications fail at execution time with
less actionable serverless errors.

IMPORTANT: Images must be public URLs or base64-encoded data.
Local file paths do NOT work — the API runs remotely and cannot
access your filesystem.

Returns workflow outputs as defined by the workflow's output blocks.

specification.description: Full Workflow JSON definition with 'version', 'inputs', 'steps', and 'outputs'

images.description: Map of input names to image values (HTTPS URLs or base64). Example: {'image': 'https://...'}

parameters.description: Optional runtime parameters defined in the workflow

tools.name: batch_processing_asset_library_job_create
tools.title: Create Asset Library Batch Processing Job
tools.description:
Queue a durable Workflow run over an Asset Library selection.

The platform owns selection authorization, entitlement and billing,
workflow compatibility, staging, and job registration: it stages your
selection into a Data Staging batch for you (for files you stage
yourself, use ``batch_processing_run`` or
``batch_processing_staged_job_start``). The response is a 202 receipt:
poll ``batch_processing_asset_library_task_get`` with its taskId until
terminal, then use ``batch_processing_job_get`` with jobId.

workflow_id.description: Published Workflow URL slug or ID.

idempotency_key.description: Stable request key, 8-128 characters. Reuse it only when retrying the same logical launch.

image_ids.description: Exact Asset Library image IDs. Use exactly one selection input.

query.description: Reviewed Asset Library RoboQL query. Use exactly one selection input.

all_images.description: Set true to explicitly select every accessible Asset Library image.

machine_type.description: Compute type; CPU is the product default.

display_name.description: Optional human-readable job name, up to 200 characters.

annotations.title: Create Asset Library Batch Processing Job

tools.name: batch_processing_asset_library_task_get
tools.title: Get Asset Library Batch Processing Task
tools.description: Poll the launch receipt until its durable job is registered.

annotations.title: Get Asset Library Batch Processing Task

tools.name: batch_processing_guide
tools.title: Batch Processing Guide
tools.description:
Route a bulk image/video processing request onto batch processing: pick the staging mode, settle the batch id, and return the exact inference-cli commands for the whole run.

Every batch processing job runs a Workflow over a Data Staging batch; the input paths differ only in who fills it. Files already in Roboflow (Asset Library): batch_processing_asset_library_job_create, and the platform selects and stages them for you. External files (local disk, cloud bucket, references file) when you only want the outputs: stage them with the inference-cli and drive the run with batch_processing_run (nothing is imported; the classic ETL shape). External files you want INSIDE Roboflow for labeling/training/curation: that is an import, not a job; mirror them with a datasource (bucket mirror, connect_cloud_storage), then run an Asset Library job over the imported images if you also want bulk predictions (the classic ELT shape).

Staging uploads are client-side: this MCP server cannot read the user's filesystem or cloud credentials, so files are staged with the inference-cli on the user's machine (pip install inference-cli). Call this with whatever you already know (local dir, bucket path, workflow, images vs videos); it returns the install line and the ordered stage/inspect/process/monitor/export commands. Read the roboflow://skills/roboflow-batch-processing/SKILL resource for the full recipe, and prefer batch_processing_run to drive the run server-side once files are staged. Requires the batch-processing feature on the workspace.

content_type.description: What the files are. Inferred from images_dir/videos_dir when given.

images_dir.description: Local directory of images to process. Optional.

videos_dir.description: Local directory of videos to process. Optional.

bucket_path.description: Cloud storage path/glob, e.g. 's3://bucket/imgs/**/*.jpg', 'gs://bucket/videos/'. Works for images and videos. Optional.

references_file.description: Path to a JSONL references file of {name, url} HTTPS entries. Optional.

workflow_id.description: Workflow to run over the batch (must exist in the workspace). Optional.

batch_id.description: Staging batch id to use (lowercase letters, digits, '-' or '_'). Optional.

tools.name: batch_processing_staging_batches_list
tools.title: List Staging Batches
tools.description:
List the workspace's data-staging batches (inputs and job results).

Returns ``{batches, nextPageToken?}``. Batches expire about 7 days
after creation. Job results appear as platform-generated batches named
``<job-id>-processing`` and ``<job-id>-export``.

next_page_token.description: Continuation token from a previous call.

tools.name: batch_processing_staging_batch_get
tools.title: Get Staging Batch
tools.description:
Get a staged batch's metadata, file count, and ingest progress.

Sharded, cloud-storage, and references ingests register files
asynchronously: the count stays low until ingest workers finish. Poll
this until ``ingest.pending`` is false and ``ingest.failed`` is false
before starting a job. For multipart batches (e.g. job results) the
response includes ``parts``.

tools.name: batch_processing_staging_batch_files_list
tools.title: List Staging Batch Files
tools.description:
List a staged batch's files with time-limited signed download URLs.

Use this to download the results of a finished job (the
``<job-id>-export`` batch). Job-result batches are multipart: when the
batch has exactly one part it is selected automatically (and echoed as
``partName``); with several parts, pass ``part_name`` (see
``batch_processing_staging_batch_get`` parts). Download URLs expire
after ~24h; archives (.tar/.tar.gz) must be unpacked after download.
Returns ``{files, returned, nextPageToken?, truncated, partName?}``.
Results are returned in whole upstream pages so ``nextPageToken``
always continues exactly where ``files`` ended. Listings are capped at
10,000 entries per call; past that, pull results with the
inference-cli's ``export-batch`` (resumable) instead.

batch_id.description: Staging batch id (job results live in '<job-id>-export')

part_name.description: Part of a multipart batch to list (see staging_batch_get parts).

limit.description: Target number of file entries to return (default 1000, cap 10000, minimum 100). The response is page-aligned and may slightly exceed the target so the returned cursor never skips files.

next_page_token.description: Continuation token from a previous call.

tools.name: batch_processing_jobs_list
tools.title: List Batch Processing Jobs
tools.description:
List the workspace's batch processing jobs.

Returns ``{jobs, nextPageToken?}`` with each job's full definition
omitted (use ``batch_processing_job_get`` for one job's detail). Each
entry carries ``inputSource``: 'asset-library' (platform-staged
selection) or 'staged-batch' (a batch the caller staged).

next_page_token.description: Continuation token from a previous call.

search.description: Optional name, Workflow or notification search (max 160 chars).

tools.name: batch_processing_job_get
tools.title: Get Batch Processing Job
tools.description:
Get a job's status and per-stage progress.

Poll this to track a running job: ``job.isTerminal`` says whether it
finished and ``job.error`` whether it failed; ``stages`` carries
per-stage progress and ``outputBatches``. When the export stage
completes, download results from the ``<job-id>-export`` staging batch
via ``batch_processing_staging_batch_files_list``.

tools.name: batch_processing_staged_job_start
tools.title: Start Batch Processing Job
tools.description:
Start a batch processing job: run a Workflow over a staged batch.

This launches asynchronous compute and consumes credits. The batch
must be staged first (see ``batch_processing_guide``) and fully
ingested (``batch_processing_staging_batch_get``). Returns
``{jobId, ...}``; poll ``batch_processing_job_get`` and fetch results
from the ``<job-id>-export`` staging batch when it finishes. Re-running
with the same job_id and identical settings is idempotent; a divergent
definition is rejected (409).

batch_id.description: Staging batch to process (must be fully ingested).

workflow_id.description: Workflow to run; must already exist in the workspace (workflows_list).

job_id.description: Stable job id (lowercase letters, digits, '-', max 20 chars). Reuse it when retrying the same request.

machine_type.description: Compute type for the workers (default cpu). Unsure? Test-run the Workflow on one image first (workflows_run; time the second call) and inspect its spec (workflows_get): one small fine-tuned model -> cpu; several chained models, large foundation models (SAM/CLIP/OCR/VLM blocks), or a test run slower than ~1s of model time -> gpu.

workers_per_machine.description: Parallel workers per machine (1, 2, 4 or 8). More workers = better utilization but a higher OOM risk.

image_input_name.description: Name of the Workflow's image input placeholder.

image_outputs_to_save.description: Only persist these image outputs (default: all).

aggregation_format.description: Format of the aggregated results file.

max_video_fps.description: Videos only: subsample predictions to at most this FPS (minimum 1).

max_image_failure_rate.description: Images only: abort when the failure rate exceeds this (0.0-1.0).

part_name.description: Multipart batches only: which part to process.

notifications_url.description: Your own webhook URL, notified when the job succeeds or fails. The platform POSTs the job notification there; this server does not receive or relay webhooks.

inference_backend.description: Execution backend. Defaults to the current product backend; use old-inference only for a known compatibility requirement.

tools.name: batch_processing_job_abort
tools.title: Abort Batch Processing Job
tools.description:
Abort a running batch processing job. Already-produced partial
results stay available in the job's staging batches.

tools.name: batch_processing_job_restart
tools.title: Restart Batch Processing Job
tools.description:
Restart a failed or aborted job, optionally overriding compute
parameters. Consumes credits like a fresh run.

machine_type.description: Override the compute type (e.g. move to gpu after an OOM or timeout).

workers_per_machine.description: Override parallel workers per machine (1, 2, 4 or 8).

max_runtime_seconds.description: Override the processing timeout, between 600 and 43200 seconds (a restart caps lower than the original job).

max_image_failure_rate.description: Images only: override the tolerated failure rate (0.0-1.0).

tools.name: batch_processing_job_logs
tools.title: Get Batch Processing Job Logs
tools.description:
Fetch a job's processing logs (paginated). Use this to diagnose
failed or slow jobs; pair with batch_processing_job_get for stage
status.

next_page_token.description: Continuation token from a previous call.

tools.name: batch_processing_run
tools.title: Run Batch Processing End To End
tools.description:
Master tool: drive a batch processing run over a staging batch you name (stage -> ingest -> job -> results) through repeated resumable calls. For Asset Library selections, use batch_processing_asset_library_job_create instead.

Every batch processing job runs a Workflow over a Data Staging batch; the input paths differ only in who fills it. Files already in Roboflow (Asset Library): batch_processing_asset_library_job_create, and the platform selects and stages them for you. External files (local disk, cloud bucket, references file) when you only want the outputs: stage them with the inference-cli and drive the run with batch_processing_run (nothing is imported; the classic ETL shape). External files you want INSIDE Roboflow for labeling/training/curation: that is an import, not a job; mirror them with a datasource (bucket mirror, connect_cloud_storage), then run an Asset Library job over the imported images if you also want bulk predictions (the classic ELT shape).

Each call reads current state, advances what it can, and returns immediately: 'staging_required' (batch missing; response contains the inference-cli commands to run), 'ingest_in_progress', 'ingest_failed', 'running' (job started or working; includes stage progress), 'completed' (includes result files with download URLs), or 'failed' (includes logs). This server never sleeps on your behalf; non-terminal responses carry retryAfterSeconds, so wait that long and call again with the returned job_id to resume; omit optional creation settings and the stored paid-job definition remains authoritative. The job is started under an id derived from (workspace, batch, workflow), so retrying after a lost response re-registers the same job rather than starting a second one. Starting the job consumes credits. For the advanced knobs (max_runtime_seconds, max_parallel_tasks, max_image_failure_rate, image_outputs_to_save) use batch_processing_staged_job_start instead.

batch_id.description: Staging batch id (lowercase letters, digits, '-' or '_').

workflow_id.description: Workflow to run; must already exist in the workspace (workflows_list).

content_type.description: What the batch contains. Defaults to images for a new run; omit when resuming to use the stored job definition.

job_id.description: Pass back the job_id from a previous call to resume monitoring. Omit on the first call; the job is started once ingest is ready under an id derived from (workspace, batch, workflow), so retrying after a lost response is safe. Passing an id that does not exist yet starts a distinct re-run of the same batch and workflow under that id, after the same ingest checks.

machine_type.description: Compute type for the workers (default cpu). Unsure? Test-run the Workflow on one image first (workflows_run; time the second call) and inspect its spec (workflows_get): one small fine-tuned model -> cpu; several chained models, large foundation models (SAM/CLIP/OCR/VLM blocks), or a test run slower than ~1s of model time -> gpu.

image_input_name.description: Name of the Workflow's image input placeholder.

save_image_outputs.description: Persist the Workflow's image outputs (crops/visualizations). Defaults to false for a new run; omit when resuming.

aggregation_format.description: Format of the aggregated results file.

max_video_fps.description: Videos only: subsample predictions to at most this FPS.

part_name.description: Required when the input is a multipart staging batch.

inference_backend.description: Execution backend. Defaults to the current product backend for a new run; omit when resuming to use the stored backend.

annotations.title: Run Batch Processing End To End

tools.name: devices_list
tools.title: List Devices
tools.description:
List devices registered in the workspace.

Returns a list of Device objects with id, name, status, last_heartbeat,
platform/hardware info, tags, and created_at. ``status`` is ``online``
if a heartbeat was received within the last 5 minutes, otherwise
``offline`` (or ``unknown`` for devices that have never reported).

Requires the ``device:read`` scope. Device-scoped api_keys cannot call
this endpoint and will receive 403.

tools.name: devices_create
tools.title: Create Device
tools.description:
Provision a new v2 device.

Requires the ``device:update`` scope. Returns
``{deviceId, installId, offlineProvisioningQrPayload?}``:
``installId`` is the short-lived token used by the device installer
(``GET /devices/v2/:installId/install.sh``).
``offlineProvisioningQrPayload`` is only present for AI1 devices
provisioned with ``offline_mode=true``.

workflow_id.description: Optional initial workflow assignment. For AI1 devices this seeds the default 'aione' stream; other device types typically bind workflows later when streams are configured.

offline_mode.description: Only valid for AI1 devices on workspaces with the roboflowLiteMode feature flag.

source_device_id.description: When set, duplicate this existing device's config instead of generating a fresh one.

tools.name: devices_get
tools.title: Get Device
tools.description:
Get a single device by id.

Returns the Device object. 404 if the device does not exist or belongs
to a different workspace.

When inspecting a device, also call ``devices_get_config`` for its
running services and ``devices_get_default_config`` for the
workspace's recommended versions — comparing the two ``services``
maps reveals whether the device is up to date or pinned to an
older build of any service.

tools.name: devices_get_config
tools.title: Get Device Config
tools.description:
Get the device's current runtime configuration.

Returns the full RFDM config JSON: ``device_id``, ``device_name``,
``workspace_id``, ``version``, ``last_updated``, ``config``,
``services``. The response passes through ``environment_variables``
and any embedded integration credentials, so treat the payload as
sensitive.

Tip: pair this with ``devices_get_default_config`` and diff the
``services`` map. The default config carries the workspace's
recommended version for each service, so comparing the two tells
you whether the device is up to date or pinned to an older build.

tools.name: devices_get_default_config
tools.title: Get Default Device Config
tools.description:
Get the workspace's default device configuration.

Returns ``{config, patch}``: ``config`` is the base default config
with the workspace's ``config_patch`` applied (the template used
when provisioning new devices, including default service versions),
and ``patch`` is the raw workspace-level patch object.

Useful for inspecting which service versions a fresh device would
be created with, or for seeding a payload to ``devices_update_config``.

Requires the ``device:read`` scope. Device-scoped api_keys are
rejected with 403 — this endpoint is workspace-wide.

tools.name: devices_update_config
tools.title: Update Device Config
tools.description:
Update the device's runtime configuration.

Requires the ``device:update`` scope. The merge is a Firestore
shallow update: omitted top-level fields stay as-is, but any
top-level field you supply replaces its entire nested object
wholesale. The payload is validated against the RFDM config
schema, and a new entry is appended to the config history.

config.description: Partial config payload. Top-level keys you include overwrite their entire nested object (no deep merge); top-level keys you omit are preserved. To change a nested value, fetch the current config with devices_get_config, splice your change into the relevant top-level object, and pass that object back here.

tools.name: devices_get_config_history
tools.title: Get Device Config History
tools.description:
List prior configuration revisions, newest first.

Returns ``{data: ConfigRevision[], pagination: {next_cursor,
has_more, limit}}``. Each ConfigRevision carries ``revision_id``,
``created_at``, and ``created_by``.

limit.description: Page size (1-500, default 10).

cursor.description: ISO timestamp from a previous page's next_cursor.

tools.name: devices_streams_list
tools.title: List Device Streams
tools.description:
List streams configured on the device.

Returns a list of Stream objects, including streams that exist only
in the device config and have not been reported by the device yet
(``status: "provisioning"``, ``provisioning: true``). ``mode`` is
``"triggered"`` for trigger-driven streams, ``"continuous"``
otherwise. Credential-bearing fields (URL userinfo, ``password``,
``credential``, etc.) are redacted from the ``source`` and
``configured_source`` fields.

tools.name: devices_streams_get
tools.title: Get Device Stream
tools.description:
Get a single stream by id.

Returns the Stream object. Streams that exist only in the device
config are returned as synthesized ``provisioning`` entries rather
than 404; 404 only if the stream exists neither live nor in config.

tools.name: devices_get_logs
tools.title: Get Device Logs
tools.description:
Fetch device logs from Elasticsearch.

Rate-limited at two tiers: 5 requests / minute per IP, and
50 requests / minute globally across all callers (Elasticsearch
protection).

Returns ``{data: LogEntry[], pagination: {next_cursor, has_more,
limit}}``.

service.description: Comma-separated service names to filter by.

limit.description: Page size (1-1000, default 100).

cursor.description: ISO timestamp from a previous page's next_cursor.

tools.name: devices_get_telemetry
tools.title: Get Device Telemetry
tools.description:
Get aggregated hardware metrics and device health sections.

Rate-limited per-device: 60 requests / minute steady, plus a
burst limit of 10 requests / 10 seconds.

By default returns ``{time_period, bucket_interval,
fill_interval_seconds, buckets, stream_fps, system_status, services,
hardware, network_interfaces, metadata}``:

- ``buckets`` — cpu/memory/disk/gpu plus
  ``network_upload_bytes_per_sec`` / ``network_download_bytes_per_sec``
- ``stream_fps`` — one series per running pipeline
  (``pipeline_id``, ``stream_name``, ``stream_id``) with a
  ``buckets`` array in ascending time order, each entry
  ``{bucket_start, camera_fps, inference_fps}``
- ``system_status`` — per-bucket docker daemon and NTP health
  (``up`` / ``partial`` / ``missing``; ``missing`` = no telemetry
  samples in that bucket)
- ``services`` — per-service container status with the latest
  container sample (image, cpu, memory); add ``service_history``
  to ``include`` for per-bucket history
- ``hardware`` — most recent startup hardware report (OS, CPU,
  Jetson/JetPack, GPU driver, uptime, NTP)
- ``network_interfaces`` — most recent interface snapshot

Pass ``include=metrics`` for the compact time-series-only response,
or ``include=stream_fps`` when you only need camera vs. inference
frame rates.

time_period.description: Aggregation window, which sets the bucket interval: 1h (2 min buckets), 24h (30 min, default), 7d (4 h), 14d (8 h).

include.description: Comma-separated sections: metrics, stream_fps, system_status, services, service_history, hardware, network_interfaces. Default is everything except service_history (per-service history arrays are large and opt-in).

tools.name: devices_get_deployments
tools.title: Get Device Deployments
tools.description:
Get the device's deployment history with per-deployment activity.

This is the device Activity tab as structured JSON: each config
revision becomes a half-open deployment window (newest window
open-ended), annotated with what happened while it was live:

- ``exception_issues`` — exceptions grouped by fingerprint with
  occurrence counts, last_seen, and the latest description; drill
  into one with ``devices_get_exception_occurrences``
- ``error_event_issues`` — error events grouped by
  entity/event/error_code
- ``execution_environment`` — the inference runtime reported during
  the window (versions, GPU, loaded models)
- ``workflow_edits`` — workflow publishes that landed mid-deployment
- ``container_pulls`` — image pulls (and failures) during the window
- ``stats`` — unique/unhandled exception counts and error event count
- ``config_changed_paths`` (opt-in) — dotted config paths changed vs
  the prior revision, values omitted
- ``trends`` (opt-in) — bucketed occurrence time series per issue

Returns ``{device_id, deployments: Deployment[], pagination:
{next_cursor, has_more, limit}}``. Prefer this over raw
``devices_get_events`` when diagnosing what a deployment broke.
Rate-limited per-device: 30 requests / minute.

limit.description: Deployments per page (1-5, default 5).

cursor.description: ISO timestamp from a previous page's next_cursor.

include.description: Comma-separated sections: issues, trends, workflow_edits, container_pulls, config_changed_paths. Default issues,workflow_edits,container_pulls.

tools.name: devices_get_exception_occurrences
tools.title: Get Exception Occurrences
tools.description:
List raw occurrences of one exception fingerprint, newest first.

Use after ``devices_get_deployments`` to see exactly when a grouped
exception fired — each row is ``{id, timestamp, error_code}``. Pair
the timestamps with ``devices_get_logs`` (``start_time`` /
``end_time`` around an occurrence) to read the surrounding log
context.

Returns ``{data: [...], pagination: {next_cursor, has_more, limit}}``.

fingerprint.description: Exception fingerprint from devices_get_deployments exception_issues. Pass the value verbatim — fingerprints embed file paths, and URL encoding is handled for you. Do not percent-encode it yourself.

limit.description: Page size (1-100, default 20).

cursor.description: Opaque cursor from a previous page.

tools.name: devices_get_snapshot
tools.title: Get Device Snapshot
tools.description:
Get the full current state of a device in one call.

Prefer this as the FIRST call when diagnosing a device — it
aggregates what would otherwise take six requests:

- ``device`` — identity, online/offline status, hardware summary,
  network interfaces, discovered cameras
- ``streams`` — ``{total, running, data}`` including config-only
  (provisioning) streams
- ``services`` / ``services_summary`` — per-service container
  status and healthy/total counts
- ``telemetry`` — the latest non-empty 1h telemetry bucket (cpu,
  memory, disk, gpu, network throughput)
- ``system_status`` — current docker daemon and NTP health
- ``hardware`` — most recent startup hardware report
- ``current_deployment`` — the live config revision with its
  exception/error issues and execution environment
- ``recent_events`` — the 20 most recent lifecycle events

Sections are best-effort: a failed section is ``null`` and named in
the top-level ``errors`` array. Follow up with the focused tools
(``devices_get_deployments``, ``devices_get_logs``,
``devices_get_telemetry``) for history and detail. The ``services``
section here is container status only. For typed sidecar state
(is the PLC connected, is the event store full) call
``devices_get_services`` or the per-sidecar tools.
Rate-limited per-device: 30 requests / minute.

tools.name: devices_get_events
tools.title: Get Device Events
tools.description:
List device and stream lifecycle events.

Returns ``{data: Event[], pagination: {next_cursor, prev_cursor,
has_more, limit}}``.

By default the feed models **state transitions**: consecutive rows
carrying the same event name for the same entity collapse into one
row unless the previous row's TTL has elapsed. That is right for
lifecycle events and wrong for periodic telemetry, which reuses a
single event name for every sample: ``plc_snapshot`` ticks every
60s with ``ttl_s: 300``, so a deduped read returns roughly one row
where the raw read returns them all.

Pass ``dedupe=False`` to read raw rows. It requires **both**
``entity_type`` and ``entity_id`` (an entity id is only unique
within its type), reports ``event_end_timestamp`` as ``null``
(an "end" is derived from the dedup window and means nothing for a
sampled reading), and is rate-limited at 30 requests / minute per
device, in the same bucket as ``devices_get_services`` and
``devices_get_service_series``. The deduped default is not
rate-limited.

For charting a named sidecar metric, prefer
``devices_get_service_series``, which resolves the entity id and the
dedup behavior for you.

entity_id.description: Filter to a single entity id.

limit.description: Page size (1-1000, default 100).

cursor.description: Opaque cursor from a previous page.

dedupe.description: Default true. Pass false to read raw rows instead of collapsed state transitions. Requires both entity_type and entity_id.

tools.name: devices_get_services
tools.title: Get Device Services
tools.description:
List the sidecar containers a device runs and what each is doing.

Joins the device's declared ``services`` config with the same
latest-value status cache the Device Manager UI subscribes to.
Returns ``{device_id, services: Service[], unassociated_signals}``.

Each Service carries ``name``, ``kind`` (resolved from the image;
an unrecognized container is ``custom``), ``image``/``tag``,
``tag_is_canonical``, ``automatic_updates``,
``has_pending_changes``, ``state`` plus ``state_reported_at`` /
``state_received_at``, ``image_state``, ``signal_conflicts``, and
the typed ``status`` for its kind.

Reading the nulls correctly:

- ``state`` and ``image_state`` are ``null`` once the last report
  has aged past its TTL; the matching ``*_received_at`` still
  carries a timestamp, so "stale reading" stays distinguishable
  from "never reported".
- ``status`` is ``null`` until the service has reported, for kinds
  that emit no telemetry (``rtsp_simulator``, ``device_hmi``,
  ``custom``), and whenever ``signal_conflicts`` is non-empty.
- ``signal_conflicts`` lists entity ids more than one declared
  service claims. Ids derive from the **kind**, so two services of
  the same kind collide unless each sets a distinct
  ``DEVICE_EVENT_ENTITY_ID``. The reading cannot be attributed, so
  it is withheld rather than guessed.
- ``unassociated_signals`` holds telemetry that matched no declared
  service (a custom container, or an entity-id override we could
  not resolve). It needs ``include=['signals']`` and is omitted
  when a ``kind`` filter is applied.

Two clocks, everywhere in this response: ``*_reported_at`` is the
device's own claim and is ``null`` when the device sent none (it is
never backfilled), while ``*_received_at`` is when the platform
recorded it. Freshness reads ``received_at``; ordering two signals
from one device reads ``reported_at``. Never compare one against
the other.

``metrics_truncated: true`` means the metrics aggregation hit its
row cap and some services report ``metrics: null`` for that reason
rather than never having reported. Narrow ``time_period``.

Rate-limited per-device: 30 requests / minute, in one bucket shared
with ``devices_get_service_series``, the per-sidecar tools, and
``devices_get_events(dedupe=False)``.

kind.description: Filter to one sidecar kind. Omit for every declared service.

include.description: Sections to return. Default ['status']. 'config' returns environment_variables verbatim (commonly PLC/broker passwords and API keys), so ask for it only when you need it. 'signals' adds the raw device-event slots behind status, and populates unassociated_signals. 'metrics' adds latest container CPU/memory.

time_period.description: Window for the 'metrics' section only. Default 24h.

tools.name: devices_get_plc_status
tools.title: Get PLC Relay Status
tools.description:
Answer "is this PLC connected?" for a device's PLC relay sidecars.

Thin view over ``devices_get_services(kind='plc_relay')``. Returns
``{device_id, services: Service[]}``; each ``status`` carries:

- ``connected``: reconciled across the every-60s snapshot and the
  transition-only connectivity events by recency, connectivity
  winning ties, so an older optimistic snapshot can never mask a
  newer disconnect. ``null`` means unknown, not disconnected: the
  two slots could not be ordered on one clock.
- ``driver``, ``plc_ip``
- ``tags`` / ``tag_count``: the tag map and its size, **withheld
  (``null``) whenever ``connected`` is not true**. Those readings
  predate the drop, and a frozen part count shown as current is how
  an operator ends up trusting a dead line.
- ``reported_at``: device clock, from the snapshot;
  ``connection_changed_at``: device clock, from the last
  connectivity transition. Both ``null`` when that slot never
  reported.
- ``stale: true``: the reading that decided ``connected`` is old
  (over 30 minutes), which is different from absent.

For connectivity history, use ``devices_get_service_series`` with
``metric='connected'`` (charts as 1/0).

service_name.description: Config name of one PLC relay service. A name that is not a PLC relay 404s. Omit to return every PLC relay declared on the device.

include_signals.description: Add the raw device-event slots behind the status, including a snapshot superseded by a newer disconnect.

tools.name: devices_get_event_store_stats
tools.title: Get Event Store Stats
tools.description:
Report a device's local event store against its capacity limits.

Thin view over ``devices_get_services(kind='event_store')``.
Returns ``{device_id, services: Service[]}``; each ``status``
carries ``records`` / ``records_limit`` / ``records_percent``,
``images``, ``bytes_used`` / ``bytes_limit`` / ``bytes_percent``,
a ``backup`` block (Vision Events upload progress: ``enabled``,
``backed_up_*``, ``pending_*``), a ``drafts`` block, ``disk``,
``capacity_blocked``, ``unuploaded_records``, and ``last_cleanup``.

Reading it correctly:

- ``capacity_blocked`` is ``null`` until the device reports a
  transition. The service emits only ``capacity_blocked`` /
  ``capacity_cleared``, so silence is genuinely unknown and
  ``false`` would assert healthy. It also reads ``true`` only while
  a fresh stats sample has not contradicted it.
- ``drafts`` is ``null`` on firmware predating the draft lifecycle,
  which is not the same as a device reporting zero drafts.
- ``stale: true`` with all counters ``null`` means no recent stats
  sample: a device that only ever reported a cleanup is not a
  healthy, current event store.
- ``reported_at`` is the device's clock and may be ``null``; the
  ``received_at`` fields are the platform's.

For a trend (fill rate, backup backlog), use
``devices_get_service_series`` with metrics such as
``records_percent``, ``bytes_percent``, ``pending_records``, or
``disk_percent_used``.

service_name.description: Config name of one event store service. A name that is not an event store 404s. Omit to return every event store declared on the device.

include_signals.description: Add the raw stats/capacity/cleanup device-event slots behind the status.

tools.name: devices_get_service_series
tools.title: Get Service Metric Series
tools.description:
Chart one named sidecar metric over time.

The metric name resolves to the right entity id, event names, and
metadata key for that service's kind, and the read skips the dedup
window that would otherwise collapse periodic telemetry. Use this
for trend questions instead of raw ``devices_get_events``.

Returns ``{device_id, service, kind, metric, metric_type,
time_period, available_metrics, truncated, covered_from,
covered_to, points: [{timestamp, value}]}``.

- ``metric_type`` is ``number`` or ``boolean``. A boolean charts as
  1/0, so the type is what tells a ``1`` meaning "true" from a
  ``1`` meaning "one".
- An unknown ``metric`` returns 400 listing the valid names for
  that kind in ``valid_values``; ``available_metrics`` on a
  successful response says the same thing.
- ``truncated: true`` means the window held more than the 5,000
  sample cap. The newest samples are kept, so ``covered_from`` /
  ``covered_to`` report the interval actually returned, which can
  be shorter than the requested window. ``plc_snapshot`` ticks
  every 60s (10,080 samples over ``7d``), so narrow the window
  for full coverage.
- Two clocks: ``time_period`` selects by when the platform
  *received* a sample, while each point's ``timestamp`` (and
  therefore ``covered_from`` / ``covered_to``) is what the device
  reported. On a badly-skewed device those can fall outside the
  requested window; that is the device's own account, not a
  filtering error.
- 409 means two services of this kind claim the same entity id, so
  the samples cannot be attributed to one of them; the response
  names the claimants.

Rate-limited per-device: 30 requests / minute, in one bucket shared
with ``devices_get_services``, the per-sidecar tools, and
``devices_get_events(dedupe=False)``.

service_name.description: Config name of the service, as returned by devices_get_services (not the kind).

metric.description: Metric name for that service's kind. event_store: records, records_percent, images, bytes_used, bytes_percent, backed_up_records, backed_up_bytes_percent, pending_records, pending_bytes, draft_records, oldest_draft_age_seconds, disk_percent_used. plc_relay: connected. opcua_server: session_count, refused_total.

time_period.description: Window, measured against platform receipt time. Default 24h.

tools.name: api_keys_list
tools.title: List API Keys
tools.description:
List all API keys for the workspace.

Secret key values are never returned — keys are represented by their
non-secret ``keyId`` handle and a masked ``prefix``. Returns
``{ api_keys, publishable_key }`` where ``publishable_key`` is the
workspace's ``rf_<workspaceId>`` key (safe to embed in client-side code).

include_disabled.description: Include disabled keys in the response

include_folders.description: Include folder details on each key

tools.name: api_keys_get
tools.title: Get API Key
tools.description:
Get metadata for a single API key by its keyId.

Secret values are never returned. The key is identified by its
non-secret ``keyId`` handle (not the secret key string).

key_id.description: The keyId of the API key to retrieve

tools.name: api_keys_get_publishable
tools.title: Get Publishable Key
tools.description:
Get the workspace's publishable key (``rf_<workspaceId>``).

The publishable key is the non-secret workspace identifier used with
Roboflow.js and browser-side inference SDKs. It is browser-safe and cannot
manage workspace data or read private resources. It is not a true secret,
but it is not powerless: anyone who holds it can run inference and download
the workspace's deployed models. Embed it in client-side code as intended;
do not treat it as a capability to hand to untrusted parties.

tools.name: api_keys_create
tools.title: Create API Key
tools.description:
Create a new API key for the workspace.

Who can create keys: a credential may create keys only if it is unscoped
(full access) or holds the ``api-key:create`` scope; an OAuth token also
needs the ``create_api_key`` permission.

Default scope — read this carefully, it is a least-privilege footgun.
Keys created in the dashboard may default to scoped (not full access), but
that dashboard default does NOT apply here. When ``scopes`` is OMITTED, an
API/MCP-created key INHERITS the calling credential's effective scopes — so
if the caller is full access, an omitted ``scopes`` produces a FULL-ACCESS
key (it comes back with ``scopes: null``). Always pass explicit
least-privilege ``scopes`` whenever you can, rather than relying on the
default.

Scopes are stored as explicit leaf scopes — a section name or ``role:``
preset is expanded to its current leaves, so a key never auto-gains an
ability added to that group later (add new scopes explicitly when needed).

The secret ``key`` value is returned ONCE in the response and cannot be
retrieved again. Store it immediately in a ``.gitignore``'d ``.env`` file
(e.g. ``ROBOFLOW_API_KEY=rf_...``). Never echo it in logs, code comments,
or tool output.

Returns ``{ key_id, key, name, scopes, folder_ids, protected, publishable_key }``.
``key_id`` is the non-secret handle used in all subsequent management calls.

scopes.description: Scope tokens restricting this key: leaf scopes (e.g. ['project:read', 'image:read']), a section name ('model' = all model scopes), or a role preset 'role:<name>' (built-in labeler/reviewer/owner or a custom role; role:owner = full access). Omit to inherit the calling credential's own scopes (so a full-access credential creates a full-access key). Providing scopes requires the Advanced API Keys plan feature.

folder_ids.description: Folder IDs this key may access. Requires the Advanced API Keys plan feature.

custom_metadata.description: Arbitrary string key/value metadata to attach to the key. Requires the Advanced API Keys plan feature.

protected.description: If true, the key cannot be revoked or disabled until it is unprotected in the Roboflow dashboard at app.roboflow.com/settings/api (the API/CLI/MCP cannot unprotect it).

tools.name: api_keys_update
tools.title: Update API Key
tools.description:
Update the name, scopes, or custom_metadata of an existing API key.

Only fields you provide are sent; omitted fields are left unchanged.
Omitting ``name`` leaves the name unchanged; omitting ``custom_metadata``
leaves the metadata unchanged. Omitting ``scopes`` leaves the key's
scopes unchanged, while passing a list replaces them entirely (including
``role:<name>`` presets). To widen a scoped key back to full access, pass
``["role:owner"]`` (subject to the usual subset rules and the Advanced API
Keys feature).

To protect or disable a key use ``api_keys_protect`` or ``api_keys_disable``.
Protection cannot be changed here (unprotecting is dashboard-only).
Returns the updated masked key metadata.

key_id.description: The keyId of the key to update

name.description: New human-readable label for the key

scopes.description: Replacement scope list (leaf scopes, a section name, or 'role:<name>' presets). Use 'role:owner' to widen the key back to full access. Requires the Advanced API Keys plan feature.

custom_metadata.description: Replacement custom metadata. Requires the Advanced API Keys plan feature.

protected.description: Not settable here. Use api_keys_protect to protect a key; unprotecting is dashboard-only and cannot be done via the API/MCP. Passing this returns guidance.

tools.name: api_keys_protect
tools.title: Protect API Key
tools.description:
Mark an API key as protected so it cannot be revoked or disabled.

Protection is one-way from the API: a protected key can only be
unprotected in the Roboflow dashboard at
``app.roboflow.com/settings/api``. The API, CLI, and MCP cannot unprotect
a key, so there is deliberately no ``api_keys_unprotect`` tool.
Returns the updated masked key metadata.

key_id.description: The keyId of the key to protect

tools.name: api_keys_disable
tools.title: Disable API Key
tools.description:
Disable (or re-enable) an API key without revoking it.

A disabled key is inactive and will be rejected by the platform until
re-enabled. Protected keys cannot be disabled; disabling requires the
Advanced API Keys plan feature, so the specific error returned depends on
the workspace. A key that backs a dedicated deployment cannot be disabled
from here either (the deployment would be paused): to rotate such a key use
``api_keys_roll``, which moves the deployment onto the replacement key.
Returns the updated masked key metadata.

key_id.description: The keyId of the key to enable or disable

disabled.description: True to disable the key; False to re-enable it

tools.name: api_keys_revoke
tools.title: Revoke API Key
tools.description:
Permanently revoke (delete) an API key.

Revocation is irreversible — the key can never be recovered or re-enabled.
Protected keys cannot be revoked; an admin must first unprotect the key in
the Roboflow dashboard at ``app.roboflow.com/settings/api``. A key that
backs a dedicated deployment cannot be revoked from here either (the
deployment would be paused): to rotate such a key — for example after a
leak — use ``api_keys_roll``, which moves the deployment onto the
replacement key. Returns ``{ status, key_id }``.

key_id.description: The keyId of the key to permanently revoke

tools.name: api_keys_roll
tools.title: Roll API Key
tools.description:
Roll (rotate) an API key: revoke it and mint a replacement in one step.

This is the rotation path for a leaked or compromised key. The replacement
keeps the old key's whole identity — name, scopes, folders, protection and
disabled state — so nothing the key was allowed to do changes; only the
secret does. Any dedicated deployment anchored on the old key is moved onto
the replacement automatically, which is why roll is allowed where
``api_keys_disable`` and ``api_keys_revoke`` refuse. The old secret stops
working immediately and its ``key_id`` is retired; the roll cannot be undone.

Protected keys cannot be rolled (unprotect in the dashboard first), and a
disabled key that backs a dedicated deployment must be re-enabled before it
can be rolled.

The new secret ``key`` is returned ONCE and cannot be retrieved again. Store
it immediately in a ``.gitignore``'d ``.env`` file and update every consumer
of the old key; never echo it in logs or tool output.

Returns ``{ key_id, key, name, scopes, folder_ids, protected, disabled,
revoked_key_id }``. ``key_id`` is the new key's non-secret handle;
``revoked_key_id`` is the handle that was rolled.

key_id.description: The keyId of the key to roll (rotate)

tools.name: vision_events_query
tools.title: Query Vision Events
tools.description:
Query production vision events for a use case, with filters and pagination.

This is the primary tool for answering questions like "what safety
alerts fired in the last week?" or "how many failed quality checks did
device X report yesterday?". Combine ``start_time``/``end_time`` with
``event_types`` for time-bounded reporting, then page with ``cursor``.

Returns ``{events, nextCursor, hasMore, lookbackDays}``. ``hasMore`` is
true when more pages exist; pass ``nextCursor`` back as ``cursor`` to
fetch them. ``lookbackDays`` is the workspace's maximum history window,
queries cannot see events older than that regardless of ``start_time``.

Each event generally carries ``eventId``, ``eventType``, ``timestamp``,
``eventData`` (type-specific), ``images`` with their detections, and
``customMetadata``. Fields such as ``deviceId``, ``streamId``,
``workflowId``, and ``displayImagePosition`` appear only when set on the
event. The use case is not echoed back per event because the result is
already scoped to the ``use_case_id`` you passed, so don't rely on a
``useCaseId``/``solution`` field being present on each event.

use_case_id.description: Use case to query (the bucket events are grouped under). Discover available ids with vision_events_use_cases_list.

start_time.description: ISO 8601 lower bound on event timestamp (e.g. '2026-06-15T00:00:00Z'). Results are also capped by the workspace's lookback window, returned as 'lookbackDays'.

end_time.description: ISO 8601 upper bound on event timestamp.

event_types.description: Filter to these event types. Valid values: quality_check, inventory_count, safety_alert, custom, operator_feedback. Max 20.

device_id.description: Only events from this device id (exact match).

stream_id.description: Only events from this stream id (exact match).

workflow_id.description: Only events from this workflow id (exact match).

limit.description: Page size (1-1000, default 100).

cursor.description: Pagination cursor from a previous page's 'nextCursor'.

additional_filters.description: Advanced structured filters merged into the query body, for cases the typed parameters above don't cover. Supported keys: 'detection' {operator: eq|neq|in|not_in, value: str|str[], confidence?: {operator: gt|gte|lt|lte, value: 0-1}}; 'customMetadataFilters' [{field, operator, value, type: string|number|boolean}]; 'eventFieldFilters' [{column: event_type|result|location|item_count|item_type|alert_type|severity|feedback|related_event_id, operator, value}]; 'externalId' {operator: eq|neq, value}; 'imageCount' {operator, value}; 'hasWarnings' bool; 'feedbackStatus' [correct|incorrect|inconclusive|none]. To match a device/stream/workflow with neq, pass it here as {operator: 'neq', value: ...} instead of the typed parameter.

tools.name: vision_events_use_cases_list
tools.title: List Vision Event Use Cases
tools.description:
List the vision-event use cases in the workspace.

Use cases are the logical buckets events are grouped under; every query
is scoped to one. Call this first to discover the ``id`` values to pass
as ``use_case_id`` to ``vision_events_query``.

Returns ``{useCases, lookbackDays}``. Each use case reliably carries
``id`` (the value to pass as ``use_case_id`` elsewhere), ``name``, and
``status``; other fields (timestamps, and any per-use-case counts or
event-type summaries) may or may not be present depending on the
workspace, so treat them as optional rather than guaranteed.

tools.name: vision_events_custom_metadata_schema_get
tools.title: Get Vision Event Custom Metadata Schema
tools.description:
Get the custom-metadata schema discovered for a use case.

Custom metadata is arbitrary key/value data attached to events at
ingestion time. This returns the fields seen so far and their value
types, which is what you need to build ``customMetadataFilters`` for
``vision_events_query``.

Returns ``{useCaseId, fields}`` where ``fields`` maps each field name to
the value types observed for it (string, number, and/or boolean).

annotations.title: Get Vision Event Custom Metadata Schema

tools.name: vision_events_use_case_create
tools.title: Create Vision Event Use Case
tools.description:
Create a new vision-event use case.

Use cases are the buckets that incoming events are grouped under.
Returns ``{id, name}``; use the returned ``id`` as ``use_case_id`` when
querying or ingesting events for this bucket.

name.description: Human-readable name for the new use case.

tools.name: vision_events_use_case_rename
tools.title: Rename Vision Event Use Case
tools.description:
Rename an existing vision-event use case.

Only the display name changes; the ``id`` and all associated events are
preserved. Returns ``{id, name}``.

tools.name: vision_events_use_case_archive
tools.title: Archive Vision Event Use Case
tools.description:
Archive a vision-event use case.

Sets the use case to ``inactive``: it is hidden from the default
``active`` listing and incoming events for it are rejected at ingestion,
so this can disrupt a live pipeline. The use case and its existing
events are preserved and it can be restored with
``vision_events_use_case_unarchive``. Returns ``{success}``.

tools.name: vision_events_use_case_unarchive
tools.title: Unarchive Vision Event Use Case
tools.description:
Restore a previously archived vision-event use case.

The reverse of ``vision_events_use_case_archive``; the use case returns
to the default ``active`` listing. Returns ``{success}``.

tools.name: universe_search
tools.title: Search Roboflow Universe
tools.description:
Search Roboflow Universe for datasets or models.

The query supports operators mixed with free-text:
- Add 'model' to only return datasets with trained models
- 'class:helmet,person' filters by class names
- 'images>500' filters by image count (also >=, <, <=)
- 'sort:stars' sorts results (stars, images, downloads, views, updated)
- 'object detection' filters by project type
- 'updated:30d' filters by recency

Example: 'fire smoke class:fire,smoke images>200 model sort:stars'

limit.description: Maximum number of results

tools.name: datasources_list
tools.title: List Datasources
tools.description:
List datasource (cloud-bucket mirror) configurations in the workspace.

Returns ``{ datasources }`` where each entry is trimmed to
``{id, name, credentialId, validated, requireVpce, latestJob}``. Use
``datasource_get`` for a single config's full detail.

tools.name: datasource_get
tools.title: Get Datasource
tools.description:
Get full detail for a single datasource, including its bucket,
mirror rules, and latest job summary.

tools.name: datasource_validate
tools.title: Validate Datasource
tools.description:
Check that Roboflow can access the datasource's bucket.

Returns ``{checks, errors}`` where ``checks`` reports whether
``listFiles``/``headFile``/``getFile`` succeeded plus a per-mirror
``headGlobFile`` result. Use it to self-diagnose a misconfigured
credential or bucket before triggering a run.

tools.name: datasource_job_get
tools.title: Get Datasource Job
tools.description:
Get the status and statistics of a single datasource mirror run.

Poll this with a ``batchId`` from ``datasource_trigger`` to track a run.
Returns the job's ``status`` (running/completed/failed), per-stage
``counters`` (enqueued/completed/failed), any ``errors``, and timestamps
(``startedAt``/``completedAt``/``lastSyncedAt``).

job_id.description: Job id (the batchId returned by datasource_trigger)

tools.name: datasource_create
tools.title: Create Datasource
tools.description:
Create a datasource that mirrors a cloud bucket into your workspace. Returns the created datasource {id}. Nothing is mirrored until you call datasource_trigger (or a schedule fires). Alternative: to only run a model/Workflow over the files and get results out, WITHOUT importing them into Roboflow, use batch processing instead (start with batch_processing_guide). Mirroring also composes with it: imported files become Asset Library images, and bulk predictions over them run as Asset Library jobs (batch_processing_asset_library_job_create). AWS/S3 assisted setup: when the user has the AWS CLI configured, help them proactively with values they may not know instead of just asking. Don't ask the user anything you can answer with the AWS CLI yourself; just run it. - Bucket: For AWS/S3, discover the bucket proactively before asking the user anything: iterate every profile from `aws configure list-profiles`, run `aws s3 ls --profile

` for each, then on the plausible candidates run `aws s3 ls s3:// --recursive --profile

| head` to see which actually contain images (and whether sidecar .json metadata sits beside them). Present a consolidated table of the image-bearing buckets (profile, path layout, file types, sidecar metadata, approx image count) and have the user pick from it. Only fall back to asking them to name a bucket if this discovery finds nothing. - Region: For AWS/S3, derive this from the chosen bucket instead of asking the user: run `aws s3api get-bucket-location --bucket ` (it returns `null`/`None` for us-east-1). Show the current AWS profile with `aws configure list`, or use `aws configure list-profiles` to show the available profiles; pass `--profile ` to select one. These commands only read non-secret metadata (profile names, bucket names, regions); never read ~/.aws/credentials or pass secret values yourself. - Credential: When a new AWS credential must be created, before handing off to the Roboflow form: resolve the AWS account for the profile in use with `aws sts get-caller-identity --profile

` (reads non-secret identity only), then give the user an account-scoped console deep-link so they land in the right account. Sign in at https://.signin.aws.amazon.com/console, then for an IAM credential create an IAM user at https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/home#/users/create, or for an AssumeRole credential create an IAM role at https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/home#/roles/create (trusting the Roboflow principal from the prerequisites docs). Collect the resulting access keys (IAM) or role ARN (AssumeRole) and enter them in the Roboflow form.

credential_id.description: Id of a stored credential (see credentials_list)

bucket_name.description:
Bucket name (without scheme or path). For AWS/S3, discover the bucket proactively before asking the user anything: iterate every profile from `aws configure list-profiles`, run `aws s3 ls --profile

` for each, then on the plausible candidates run `aws s3 ls s3:// --recursive --profile

| head` to see which actually contain images (and whether sidecar .json metadata sits beside them). Create a cloud-storage credential.

The secret (keys, service-account JSON, password, etc.) is never entered
in chat. This returns ``manual_entry_required`` with a ``url`` to create
the credential in the Roboflow app, a ``docs_url`` for help, and (for AWS

account-scoped console deep-link to create the IAM user/role, then enter

credential_type, description) are passed as arguments here.

the ``docs_url`` prerequisites walk through creating either an IAM user

profile and has the AWS CLI configured, you may run ``aws configure
list-profiles`` locally to list profile names and help them pick one

yourself). Either way the user enters the secret in the Roboflow app
form that ``url`` opens; nothing secret passes through you.
